analysis.one_liner: Makes home-based care for disabled and older Medicaid recipients a guaranteed benefit instead of a scarce, waitlisted one.
analysis.headline: The HCBS Access Act, which would have made home care a guaranteed Medicaid benefit, died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, Medicaid covers care in a nursing home in every state, but help at home — a home health aide, a personal care attendant, transportation, home modifications — is optional, limited by waiting lists, and requires constant federal waiver applications. This bill would have made those home and community-based services a required Medicaid benefit for anyone with a qualifying disability, with the federal government covering 100% of the cost during a five-year transition. It also would have funded recruitment and training of the direct care workforce, supported family caregivers, and permanently extended programs that help people move out of institutions. It never received a hearing, a vote, or a cost estimate; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Disabled people and older adults who need help with daily living would gain the right to receive care at home instead of being warehoused in nursing homes or stuck on years-long waiting lists. Their families — roughly 53 million unpaid family caregivers, per the bill's own findings — would get respite and support. Direct care workers, a workforce of nearly 2.6 million that is mostly low-paid women of color, would gain federal recognition, training grants, and state commitments to a living wage.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Disabled people, older adults, family caregivers

how_it_helps.text: Requires every state Medicaid program to cover home and community-based services — help at home with bathing, dressing, meals, transportation, and community participation — as a guaranteed benefit for people with qualifying disabilities.

Phases out the state-by-state waiver system that currently forces people to wait on long lists, and covers people based on a functional assessment rather than income alone, with a new eligibility path up to 150% of poverty (or 300% of the SSI rate) so more disabled adults qualify.
Has the federal government pay 100% of the cost of home and community-based services, removing the financial incentive that currently pushes states toward cheaper nursing homes.

Funds a technical assistance center and grants to recruit, train, and advance direct care workers, and requires states to plan for a living wage for those workers; it also creates a separate federal occupational code for direct support professionals.
Extends protections against spousal impoverishment for people receiving home-based care and makes the Money Follows the Person program, which helps people leave institutions, permanent.

analysis.who_pays: Federal and state taxpayers would pay for the expanded coverage. The bill has the federal government pick up 100% of home and community-based services costs, an open-ended entitlement with no stated spending cap, while states must expand services and pay enough to attract workers. Nursing homes and other institutional providers would also face the cost of losing residents to home-based alternatives.

drawbacks.text: Making home and community-based services a mandatory Medicaid benefit with a 100% federal match would commit the federal government to a large, ongoing share of long-term care spending, at a scale the bill's sponsors never got to defend in a cost estimate.

The bill would take effect only five years after enactment and gives the Secretary authority to let states keep operating waivers past that date, so full coverage for people on waiting lists could arrive slowly and unevenly.

By sunset of the state waiver system, the bill would shift authority for these services heavily toward the federal government and a mandatory benefit, reducing state flexibility over how long-term care is delivered — a genuine concern for states worried about future federal cost-shifting.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main drawback is cost: making home care a mandatory Medicaid benefit with the federal government picking up 100% of the tab for a five-year transition period would shift hundreds of billions in long-term care spending to federal taxpayers, with open-ended costs after that since states would face an entitlement they cannot cap. Opponents would also note that mandating a service without first fully funding the workforce could strain the same workers the bill tries to help. On the other side, the status quo it would replace is expensive too — nursing facilities are one of the costliest forms of long-term care, and families currently shoulder enormous unpaid caregiving burdens. The bill was never debated or scored publicly, so no official cost estimate or legislative compromise ever sharpened these tradeoffs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to three House committees, then parked in the Energy and Commerce health subcommittee, where no hearing or markup ever moved it forward before the term ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 9, 2023, and referred to the Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, and Oversight committees.
On March 17, 2023, it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health — the last action ever taken on the bill.
No further action was recorded through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025: no hearings, no markup, no floor vote, and no Senate companion movement appears in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: States that would have had to expand and fund home-based care, and the fiscal status quo generally, are better off because the bill never advanced. Also better off are institutional care providers who would have lost residents to home-based alternatives. Disabled people on waiting lists and underpaid care workers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State budgets and the care-status quo

for.name: Rep. Debbie Dingell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the HCBS Access Act and championed making home and community-based care a mandatory Medicaid benefit.

for.name: 12 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of the bill; no Republican cosponsored it in the House.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral but took no action after assigning it to the Health Subcommittee — no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce and Oversight Committees
against.what_they_did: Also received the bill by referral and took no recorded action on it.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 supporters in the record were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never advanced far enough for a floor vote that would have shown where members of either party actually stood.

industries.industry: Home care agencies and direct care providers
industries.note: The bill would send a large new stream of Medicaid funding their way and fund workforce grants, but it also demands competitive wages, quality reporting, and a bigger, better-paid workforce — costs that low-wage care businesses would have to absorb.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and institutional care facilities
industries.note: By guaranteeing home-based care as a Medicaid entitlement and permanently extending Money Follows the Person, the bill would let many people leave or avoid institutions, shifting residents and revenue toward home care. That competition is the point: people with disabilities and older adults would no longer be pushed into facilities.

industries.industry: Direct care workers (home health aides, personal care and direct support professionals)
industries.note: The bill would fund training, apprenticeships, and career ladders, direct states to ensure a living wage, and give the occupation its own federal classification — the kind of recognition that tends to raise pay and standards in a workforce that is predominantly women of color earning near minimum wage.

States would gain an implementation grant but then bear the obligation to expand and staff home-based services; the bill imposes new planning, quality, and reporting requirements, and the full-coverage mandate is backed by a state plan requirement rather than an opt-out.
